topics.title: Ruskin Bond and his world of hills

learn.hook: Imagine a writer who looks out of his window at the mountains every morning and turns what he sees into stories. Meet Ruskin Bond!
points: 'The Cherry Tree' is a story by Ruskin Bond about a boy who plants a cherry seed and patiently watches it grow through the seasons and the years.
Ruskin Bond is an Indian author, born on 19 May 1934 in Kasauli, Himachal Pradesh. He has lived for many years in Landour, Mussoorie, in Uttarakhand.
He writes about the hills, trees, birds, small-town life and children, in simple, warm language. His first novel, 'The Room on the Roof', was written when he was a teenager.
His well-known works include 'The Blue Umbrella', the Rusty stories, and 'Our Trees Still Grow in Dehra', which won the Sahitya Akademi Award. He has received the Padma Shri and the Padma Bhushan.
His stories often show that small, everyday things, like a seed or a bird, hold great joy if we notice them.

example.q: Read this original passage: 'Tara pressed an apricot stone into the soil behind her house in Almora. For weeks nothing happened. She almost forgot it. Then one rainy morning she spotted two tiny green leaves pushing up through the earth, and she laughed out loud.' Think it through: what does Tara's laugh tell us, and what is the theme?
steps: For weeks nothing happened, so Tara had to wait.
When the leaves appeared, she laughed out loud: she was delighted.
The joy came after a long wait.
So the theme is that patience is rewarded with the joy of growth.
example.answer: Her laugh shows delight; the theme is that patience brings the joy of seeing something grow.

learn.reallife: Planting a seed in a pot on your balcony and checking it every day is a small lesson in patience, just like in Bond's stories.

topics.title: Patience and growth: words of a growing tree

learn.hook: A tree does not grow when you shout at it. It grows a little every day while you wait. What words describe that journey?
points: A tree's life: a seed germinates (sprouts), becomes a seedling, then a sapling (a young tree), then a grown tree that flowers and bears fruit.
Growth words: bud (an unopened flower or leaf), blossom (flowers of a fruit tree), bloom (to flower), wither (to dry up and shrink), prune (to cut off extra branches).
Patience is the ability to wait calmly. Patient (adjective) → patience (noun) → patiently (adverb). The opposite is impatient/impatience.
Words related to patience: perseverance (keeping on trying), endurance (bearing difficulty). Proverb: 'Rome was not built in a day.'
Growth stories teach that care, time and hope together make things grow, whether it is a tree or a skill.

example.q: Think it through: Put the life of a fruit tree in order: sapling, seed, fruit, seedling, flowers.
steps: Everything begins with a seed.
The seed sprouts into a seedling.
The seedling grows into a sapling, a young tree.
The grown tree flowers.
The flowers turn into fruit.

learn.reallife: Learning to play the tabla, ride a bicycle or speak a new language also grows slowly, one small step at a time.

quiz.q: What is a sapling?
quiz.explain: A sapling is a young tree, older than a seedling.
steps: A sapling is older than a seedling but still small.
It is a young tree.
Answer: A young tree
quiz.mistake: Confuses sapling with seed or seedling

quiz.q: Which comes first in a plant's life?
quiz.explain: A plant's life begins with a seed.
steps: A plant's life cycle: seed → seedling → sapling → tree with blossom and fruit.
It begins with a seed.
Answer: Seed
quiz.mistake: Does not think about the life cycle order

quiz.q: 'Without water, the plant began to ___.' Choose the best word.
quiz.explain: Plants without water dry up and shrink: they wither.
steps: Plants without water dry up and shrink.
That is 'wither'; bloom, blossom and sprout mean growing.
Answer: wither
quiz.mistake: Chooses a word of healthy growth

quiz.q: What is the opposite of 'patience'?
quiz.explain: Patience → impatience (with the prefix im- before p).
steps: Before 'p', the opposite prefix is usually im-.
Patience → impatience.
Answer: impatience
quiz.mistake: Uses the wrong negative prefix

quiz.q: Choose the adverb: 'She waited ___ for the seed to sprout.'
quiz.explain: 'Waited' is a verb, and an adverb describes how she waited: patiently.
steps: 'Waited' is a verb; a word telling how she waited is an adverb.
patient + -ly = patiently.
Answer: patiently
quiz.mistake: Uses the adjective or noun instead of the adverb

quiz.q: What does 'germinate' mean?
quiz.explain: A seed germinates when it starts to grow and sends out a shoot.
steps: 'Germinate' describes what a seed does when it starts to grow.
It means to sprout from a seed.
Answer: To sprout from a seed
quiz.mistake: Confuses germinate with other gardening actions

quiz.q: Which proverb is about patience?
options: Rome was not built in a day.
Too many cooks spoil the broth.
Don't judge a book by its cover.
Birds of a feather flock together.
quiz.explain: It means big things take time, so we must be patient.

Answer: Rome was not built in a day.

quiz.q: Which word is a synonym of 'perseverance'?
quiz.explain: Perseverance means continuing to try with determination.
steps: Perseverance means continuing to try with determination.
So its synonym is determination.
Answer: determination
quiz.mistake: Picks an antonym

teach.ask: Gappu planted a seed yesterday and is upset that there is no tree today! What should he know?
teach.praise: Okay, okay, I'll wait! A seed becomes a seedling, then a sapling, slowly over time with care. Patience, Gappu!
teach.nudge: Does a tree grow in one day? What steps does a seed go through, and what do I need while I wait?

revise.summary: A tree grows from seed to seedling to sapling to a grown tree that flowers and bears fruit. Patience, care, time and hope make things grow, whether a tree or a skill.

perseverance (keeping on trying), endurance (bearing difficulty); 'Rome was not built in a day.'

topics.title: Time and growth: present perfect with since and for

learn.hook: 'The tree grew' is finished. 'The tree has grown' connects the past to now. One small helping verb, a big difference!
points: The present perfect tense = has/have + past participle: The tree has grown taller. We have planted ten saplings.
Use it for actions in the past whose result matters now, or for actions that began in the past and continue until now.
Use 'for' with a period of time (for three years, for two weeks) and 'since' with a point in time (since 2022, since Monday, since morning).
Do not use the present perfect with a finished past time like 'yesterday' or 'last year'. Say 'I planted it last year', not 'I have planted it last year'.
Present perfect continuous (has/have been + verb-ing) stresses that an action is still going on: It has been raining since morning.

example.q: Think it through: Fill in with 'since' or 'for': 'Rohan has watered the cherry tree every day ___ June. He has cared for it ___ four months.'
steps: June is a point in time, so use 'since'.
Four months is a length of time, so use 'for'.

learn.reallife: We use this tense to share news: 'I have finished my project!' 'Our school has won the trophy!'

items.text: The sapling ___ grown a lot this year.
We have ___ twenty trees in our school garden.
My grandparents have lived in Shimla ___ forty years.

quiz.q: Which sentence is in the present perfect tense?
quiz.explain: Has + past participle (grown) makes the present perfect.
steps: Present perfect = has/have + past participle.
'The tree has grown tall' fits ('grew' is simple past).
Answer: The tree has grown tall.
quiz.mistake: Confuses present perfect with simple past

quiz.q: Choose the correct option: 'I have lived here ___ 2019.'
quiz.explain: 2019 is a point in time, so use 'since'.
steps: 2019 is a point in time.
Points in time take 'since'.
Answer: since
quiz.mistake: Uses 'for' with a point in time

quiz.q: Choose the correct option: 'She has practised the sitar ___ two hours.'
quiz.explain: Two hours is a length of time, so use 'for'.
steps: Two hours is a length (period) of time.
Periods take 'for'.
Answer: for
quiz.mistake: Uses 'since' with a period of time

quiz.q: Which sentence is correct?
options: I have seen the cherry blossoms yesterday.
I saw the cherry blossoms yesterday.
I have saw the cherry blossoms yesterday.
I seen the cherry blossoms yesterday.
quiz.explain: 'Yesterday' is a finished past time, so use the simple past 'saw'.
steps: 'Yesterday' is a finished past time.
Finished past time takes the simple past: 'I saw the cherry blossoms yesterday.'
Answer: I saw the cherry blossoms yesterday.
quiz.mistake: Uses the present perfect with a finished past time

quiz.q: Complete: 'They ___ just finished planting the saplings.'
quiz.explain: 'They' takes 'have': They have just finished.
steps: The present perfect uses has/have; 'they' is plural.
Plural subjects take 'have'.
Answer: have
quiz.mistake: Uses 'has' with a plural subject

quiz.q: Which sentence uses the present perfect continuous?
options: It has been raining since morning.
quiz.explain: Has been + raining shows an action that started earlier and is still going on.
steps: Present perfect continuous = has/have been + verb-ing.
'It has been raining since morning' fits.
Answer: It has been raining since morning.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with the present continuous

quiz.q: What is the past participle of 'grow'?
quiz.explain: grow-grew-grown. The present perfect uses 'grown': has grown.
steps: The forms are grow – grew – grown.
The past participle is grown.
Answer: grown
quiz.mistake: Uses the simple past 'grew' after 'has'

quiz.q: Choose the correct option: 'Our neighbour ___ looked after the garden since last winter.'
quiz.explain: 'Since last winter' needs the present perfect, and the singular subject takes 'has'.
steps: 'Since last winter' needs the present perfect (has/have + past participle).
'Our neighbour' is singular, so 'has'.
Answer: has
quiz.mistake: Uses the past tense with 'since'

teach.ask: Gappu asks: When do I say 'since' and when do I say 'for'? And what is 'has grown'?
teach.praise: Got it! 'Since' with a starting point, 'for' with a length of time, and 'has grown' is the present perfect!
teach.nudge: Is '2020' a point in time or a length of time? Which word goes with it? And what makes 'has grown' special?

revise.summary: The present perfect (has/have + past participle) is for past actions whose result matters now, or actions that began in the past and continue. Use 'for' with a period of time and 'since' with a point in time.
focus: Form the present perfect and present perfect continuous.
Avoid the present perfect with a finished past time.
remember: Present perfect = has/have + past participle: The tree has grown taller.
for + period (for three years); since + point in time (since 2022, since Monday).
Present perfect continuous: has/have been + verb-ing: It has been raining since morning.
traps: Don't use the present perfect with 'yesterday' or 'last year': 'I planted it last year'.
Don't mix up 'for' (period) and 'since' (point in time).
